newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch submits plan on voting to IGC.
newsitem.headline: Dutch submits plan on voting to IGC.

text.p: The number of proposals that need a unanimous vote to become law in the European Union could be greatly reduced under a plan unveiled on Tuesday, as the inter-governmental conference broached one of its most sensitive subjects.

The cautious title of the proposal submitted by the Dutch EU presidency to EU foreign ministers' personal representatives underlined just how explosive the issue is, especially in Britain which insists on keeping its veto over EU proposals.

Headed "provisions which could form a working basis for examining a possible extension of qualified majority voting", the paper outlines 25 articles of the EU treaty where the veto could be abandoned in favour of qualified majority voting.

They range from the right of movement and residence through industry, culture and the environment to the adoption of the EU's research framework programme and compensatory aid for imports of raw materials.
They also covered approximation of common market laws where article 100a is not applicable, specific action outside the structural funds and financial regulation.

Dutch Secretary of State for European Affairs Michiel Patijn said there seemed to be general agreement that the right of veto should not be touched when it came to constitutional matters, exemptions from the EU's single market and matters with a direct impact on EU expenditure and income.
The proposed list of areas which could be settled by qualified majority was more tricky.
"There was a general agreement on the approach, but there was a lot of small print from the member states. We are not yet out of the woods," Patijn told reporters after the meeting.
Britain's European Affairs Minister David Davis said last week that those who hoped a change of government would prompt a British change of approach to its veto risked disappointment.
The EU's inter-governmental review of its workings is scheduled to wind up at the Amsterdam European Council on June 16-17 and by that time Britons could have voted for a change of government.

Patijn stressed that there was no question of moving from unanimity to qualified majority on taxation matters and said Tuesday's talks did not broach the issue of voting on the EU's second and third pillars covering respectively foreign and security policy and justice and home affairs issues.
Those issues will be the subject of separate talks, Patijn said.
The meeting also discussed, but did not reach a conclusion on flexibility, voting weightings, fundamental human rights and non-discrimination.
